opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to figure out where your value comes from that **won't be eaten by the next model.**

Many agent startups right now are building a lot of scaffolding: prompt engineering, workflow orchestration, all kinds of tricks to make the current model work a bit better. That's useful in the short term, but a lot of it gets wiped out once the base model improves. If your core competitiveness is "I patched over a weakness of GPT-4," that moat is very thin.

So I'd ask founders to think about a few things.

**First, the environment and the context.** The model is becoming a commodity, but the environment it operates in, the tools it can access, and the context it understands about a specific user or organization are not. If you own a unique environment or deeply understand a particular workflow, that's something a general model can't easily replace.

**Second, the data flywheel, or more precisely, the feedback loop.** Agents are different from chatbots because they take actions and get results from the world. If your product naturally collects signals about what succeeded and what failed, and you can use that to keep improving, that compounds over time. It's a form of learning that sits outside the model weights.

**Third, choosing the right task.** I often think about the "second half" of AI. In the first half, people focused on training better models and beating benchmarks. Now the more important question is: what problem is actually worth solving, and how do you evaluate whether you've solved it? A lot of agent products fail not because the model is too weak, but because the task definition is vague, or the evaluation doesn't reflect real utility. Founders should spend much more time defining what "good" looks like for their users.

**Finally, interaction design.** Agents change the relationship between humans and computers. It's not just "type a question, get an answer." It's delegation, trust, and collaboration over long time horizons. How much autonomy do you give the agent? When should it come back to the human? How do you build trust? These are product questions, not model questions, and I think there's huge room for innovation there.

So in one sentence: don't compete with the model, ride the model. Build on things that get *more* valuable as models get stronger, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says founders’ most important priority is figuring out where their value comes from beyond what the next model provides, and ties that value to real utility for users.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to be really honest with yourself about where the capability frontier actually is, and build right at that edge, not behind it and not too far ahead of it.

A lot of founders fall into one of two traps. The first is building thick scaffolding around a model to compensate for things the model can't do today. That works for a quarter, maybe two, and then the next model release makes most of that scaffolding unnecessary or even harmful, because you've constrained the model in ways that stop it from using its new abilities. The second trap is the opposite: betting on a capability that isn't there yet and burning a year waiting for it. So the question I'd ask is, if the model got twice as good next year, does my product get twice as good, or does it get obsoleted? You want to be in the first category.

The second thing, and I'd say this is where most of the value is, is environments and evaluation. Everyone talks about models and agents, but the thing that's actually scarce is a well-defined task with a real feedback signal. If you can describe your domain as an environment, meaning here is the state, here are the actions, here is how we know whether the agent succeeded, then you have something both the model and your team can improve against. Most real-world work is not like that yet. It's messy, the success criteria are implicit, and the feedback loop is slow. Founders who do the unglamorous work of making that loop fast and legible will end up with a moat, because the data and the evals they accumulate are things a general model lab doesn't have.

And related to that, I'd focus less on demos and more on reliability. An agent that works 80 percent of the time in a demo is very impressive and almost useless in production. Going from 80 to 99 is where the product is, and it's mostly about understanding failure modes, which again means you need good environments and good evals.

The last thing I'd say is about choosing the domain. Pick something where the person using it can verify the result cheaply, where mistakes are recoverable, and where there's a lot of repetition. Coding is the obvious example and that's why it got there first. But there are many other places with that same structure, and I think there's a lot of room for people who know a specific industry deeply and can translate it into something an agent can be trained and measured on.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes building at the model capability frontier and creating strong environments and evaluations. It does not identify clarifying the incremental value founders bring to users as the most important priority.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to find a problem where you can close the loop: the agent does something, you can tell whether it worked, and you can use that feedback to improve it. A demo that looks impressive is very different from a product someone relies on every day.

So I would start with the user’s workflow. Where do they spend time? Which steps can the agent actually take over? What happens when it makes a mistake? Sometimes a narrower agent that reliably completes one valuable task is much more useful than a general agent that can attempt everything.

You also have to think about what happens as the underlying models improve. You want better models to make your product more valuable. Understanding the customer, integrating into their workflow, and having a good way to measure success give you a foundation you can keep building on.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes finding a task with measurable feedback and understanding the user’s workflow. It does not clearly identify clarifying the agent’s incremental value to users as the founders’ most important priority.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to find a task where you can close the loop. The agent does something, you can tell whether it succeeded, and you can use that feedback to improve it. A demo can look impressive, but a product has to deliver value repeatedly.

So I would start with a concrete user and a concrete workflow. What are they trying to accomplish? Where do they spend time? What would make them trust the agent enough to delegate that work? Sometimes the bottleneck is model capability, but sometimes it’s the tools, the interface, or how the agent asks for help.

And I’d think carefully about what happens as models improve. If a better model comes out tomorrow, does your product become more useful? Ideally, you’re building the workflow, the feedback, and the relationship with users that let you turn that improvement into real value.

r001.rationale: The candidate prioritizes finding a task with a measurable feedback loop and delivering repeated value. It does not clearly identify clarifying the founders’ incremental value to users as the most important priority.
